title: Two books for one camp
hookLine: a Persian poet and a Roman emperor, read side by side, each in his own world

cards: Two men who could never have met. One is a Roman emperor in a cold army camp by the Danube river, around the year 170, writing at night by lamplight in a private notebook, reminding himself how to be a decent person.
The other is a Muslim scholar in the city of Konya, in what is now Turkey, a thousand years later, reciting long poems full of stories while a student writes them down. One speaks Greek, one Persian.
One leans on reason, the other on longing for God. For the next seventy-five days, you'll read them side by side.

teach.b: The first book is the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. You've already met him: the view from above, the morning preview.
He wrote it in Greek, not Latin, in twelve short books, and most scholars think he never meant anyone else to read it.
The oldest manuscripts give it a title that means simply to himself; the name Meditations was added much later.
So you're reading someone's private notes: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself," one well-known entry starts, and then lists the difficult people he expects to meet.
The second book is the Masnavi of Jalal al-Din Rumi.

teach.h: THE MASNAVI: SIX BOOKS OF STORIES.
teach.b: It's enormous, about twenty-five thousand couplets in six books, in Persian, full of stories: merchants, parrots, kings, lovers, a reed flute.

Rumi was a Muslim scholar and a teacher of Islamic law, steeped in the Qur'an, and the Masnavi is soaked in it. Some Persian speakers have called it the Qur'an in Persian, a phrase that tells you how deeply it's loved.
Here's how this camp works. You'll read in paraphrase and in careful older translations, one story or one passage at a time.
Each man stays in his own world. Marcus is a Stoic who trusts reason and duty. Rumi is a Muslim mystic who speaks of longing for God.
I won't pretend they're saying the same thing, and I won't make one of them the winner.
Just listen to each, and notice what happens in you when two different voices sit side by side.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often read a short entry each morning, and readers of Rumi's Masnavi traditionally read it slowly, story by story, sometimes in study circles, especially in Turkey, Iran and South Asia.

practice: If you can, pick up two real books, any two, one in each hand; if not, rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and imagine them. Feel the weight of each: different sizes, different worlds.
Don't choose between them; just hold both, and let your breath move between your hands.
